phonemes.desc: Voiced velar stop [ɡ] as in English 'give', short close [i], and the long geminate nasal [nː] of ginn-; the doubled n is held, as in modern Icelandic.
Short back [u], then the velar nasal [ŋ] of ng before the stop — Old Norse writes the cluster as it sounds.
Hard [ɡ] again at the head of the second element, short open [a], final unaspirated [p]; the whole second element is the everyday Old Norse noun gap, 'chasm, yawning void'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'GIN-noong-ahp' — stress the first syllable, hold the double n long, keep the u of -ng- short as in 'put', and end with a hard g and a clipped final p.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: ginnungagap, the neuter compound 'gap of the ginnungs'; Völuspá's own word order is gap ginnunga (st. 3).

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: ginnungagap, the learned word for the primordial void, kept alive from the medieval corpus.

kin.label: English
kin.form: gap — a Viking-Age loan from Old Norse gap; the second element of the compound still yawns in every English sentence.

kin.label: Germanic kin
kin.form: Old Norse ginna 'to deceive, bewitch' and ginnregin 'the mighty (magic-charged) powers' — the disputed first element.

pronunciation.note: Ginnungagap is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. Only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input; the void was never hard to type, only hard to imagine.

domains.title: Primordial Void
domains.subtitle: The Yawning Gap Where Rime Met Flame Before the World Began
domains.lead: Ginnungagap is the emptiness that was there first: the vast, mild, windless chasm between Niflheimr's rime and fog in the north and Muspellsheimr's fire and sparks in the south, in whose middle the two extremes met, melted, and quickened into Ymir — the condensation from which the whole made world, and the Æsir themselves, descend.

cards.name: Niflheimr
cards.desc: The world of fog and rime in the north, made long before the earth — its spring Hvergelmir feeds the rivers called the Élivágar.

cards.name: Muspellsheimr
cards.desc: The burning world in the south, bright and impassable to any not native to it, where Surtr stands at the frontier with a flaming sword.

cards.name: The Meeting
cards.desc: Where the sparks and embers flying from the south touched the rime drifting from the north, the gap thawed, dripped — and the drops took on life.

cards.name: Ymir
cards.desc: The first shape the void made: the frost-ogre who quickened in the meltwater, called Aurgelmir by the rime-giants who descend from him.

symbols.name: The gap itself
symbols.meaning: Emptiness as precondition — the room in which opposites can meet and anything at all can begin

symbols.name: Rime and spark
symbols.meaning: The two extremes the void holds apart and joins — ice from Niflheimr, embers from Muspellsheimr

symbols.name: The quickening drops
symbols.meaning: Life condensing out of the meltwater where the two worlds' weather collided

symbols.name: The windless mildness
symbols.meaning: Snorri's strange detail that Ginnungagap was as mild as a windless sky — the void is neutral, not hostile

mythology.lead: Ginnungagap has no adventures, because it is not a character but a place — or rather the condition of there being places at all. Its mythology is the first chapter of everything: the Norse creation, told in Völuspá's three terse lines and unpacked by Snorri into the finest cosmogony the Germanic world preserved.

myths.title: The Gap of Ginnungs
myths.text: The seeress reaches back before memory: 'Early in time, when Ymir made his settlement — there was no sand nor sea nor cool waves; earth was found nowhere, nor the sky above; a gap of ginnungs there was, but grass nowhere.' That is the entire notice the oldest poem gives, and everything Snorri builds hangs on its two words, gap ginnunga. No god speaks, nothing acts; the poem simply registers an emptiness where the world will later be, with the first giant already housed at its edge.

myths.title: Fog in the North, Fire in the South
myths.text: Asked what was before the earth, Hár tells Gylfi that Niflheimr was made many ages before the world: a dark world of mist with the spring Hvergelmir at its heart, from which run the rivers called the Élivágar — Svǫl, Gunnþrá, Fjǫrm, Fimbulþul, Slíðr and Hríð, Sylgr and Ylgr, Víð, Leiptr, and Gjǫll, which flows nearest the gate of Hel. Far from that spring the rivers hardened like the slag that runs from a forge, turned to ice, and spread rime and freezing fog northward. But the southern part of Ginnungagap faced Muspellsheimr, the bright, burning world no foreigner can enter, where Surtr stands guard at the border with a flaming sword — and the sparks and glowing embers that flew out of Muspellsheimr lightened the gap from below.

myths.title: The Mild Void and the Quickening
myths.text: Between the two, Snorri says, Ginnungagap was as mild as a windless sky. Where the warm air from the south met the rime from the north, the ice thawed and dripped — and by the power of the one who sent the heat, the running drops quickened and took the likeness of a man. He is named Ymir, though the rime-giants call him Aurgelmir, and from him their whole race descends; asked whether Ymir was a god, Hár answers flatly that he and all his kin were evil. From the same rime-drops came the cow Auðhumla, whose four rivers of milk fed the giant, and who licked the salty rime-stones until, over three days, a man emerged whole from the ice: Búri, the grandfather of the gods.

myths.title: The Flood and the Fashioning
myths.text: Búri's son Borr married Bestla, daughter of the giant Bǫlþorn, and their sons were Óðinn, Vili, and Vé — and the first act of the new gods in the old void was a killing. They slew Ymir, and so much blood ran from his wounds that the whole race of rime-giants drowned, save one: Bergelmir, who climbed with his wife onto his lúðr — a word that may mean a boat or a chest — and from whom the giants of the frost descend anew. The brothers dragged Ymir's body into the middle of Ginnungagap and made the world of it: the earth from his flesh, the sea and lakes from his blood, the mountains from his bones and teeth, the sky from his skull, held up at the four corners by the dwarfs Norðri, Suðri, Austri, and Vestri, and the clouds from his brains. The sparks that flew out of Muspellsheimr they set in the sky as stars. Thus the gap was not filled so much as furnished: everything that exists is a giant's body arranged inside the old emptiness.

myths.title: The Poets' Version
myths.text: The Poetic Edda confirms Snorri's outline from its own witnesses. Vafþrúðnir the giant, questioned by Óðinn about the first origin of giantkind, answers that out of the Élivágar sprang poison-drops that grew until a giant came from them. And Grímnismál gives the fashioning in verse: 'From Ymir's flesh the earth was shaped, and the mountains from his bones; the sky from the skull of the frost-cold giant, and from his blood the sea' — and adds that the gracious powers made Miðgarðr for men's sons from his eyebrows, and the hard-mooded clouds from his brains. The poems do not name the gap as often as Snorri does, but they supply its inventory: ice-rivers, venom, melt, and a world assembled from a corpse.

lore.syncretism: The obvious cross-border twin is Hesiod's Chaos: 'first of all came Chaos' opens the Greek theogony, and the Greek word itself derives from a root meaning 'to yawn, gape' — chaos and gap are the same image in two languages, the world beginning as an open mouth. The parallel is real but easy to overdraw: Hesiod's Chaos is a begetter, parent of Erebos and Night, while Ginnungagap begets nothing by itself — it is the neutral stage on which rime and fire do the begetting, and the North reserves the making for the gods who arrive later. Scholars such as Lindow have set the Norse account among the broader Indo-European creation patterns — the primordial being dismembered into the world has cousins from Vedic Puruṣa onward — but the void itself, cold at one end and burning at the other, is the corpus's own signature.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ginnungagap is the rare cosmological term that never had to be revived, because it was never allowed to die: Modern Icelandic keeps ginnungagap as its word for the primordial void, and Icelandic science writing reaches for it when describing the nothing before the Big Bang. The nineteenth-century Norse revival made the scene a set-piece — the Kearys' The Heroes of Asgard (1857) opens its cosmology in 'the great gulf' between ice and fire — and every handbook since, from Simek to Orchard, has treated the word as the North's answer to chaos. Modern Heathenry honours the creation narrative as its cosmogony, and popular culture borrows the name wherever a story needs a primal abyss, from Marvel's Thor comics to fantasy games. Its deepest legacy is conceptual: the idea, natural to the North, that the precondition of creation is not a maker's word but an empty space where opposites can meet.
lore.extendedMeditation: Every cosmogony must answer the same rude question: what was there before anything was? The North's answer is the strangest and, in its way, the most honest — room. Not a god, not a word, not even darkness with a personality: a gap, mild as a windless sky, with ice weather at one end and fire weather at the other. Creation, in this telling, is not commanded; it condenses. Two climates that could never touch are given somewhere to meet, and the world is what drips out of the meeting. Ginnungagap asks a quieter question than most voids: not what made you, but what made room for you — and it suggests that every beginning, cosmological or personal, starts the same way: with an emptiness patient enough to hold the opposites apart until they are ready to collide.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Ginnungagap — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the compound would have been carved ᚴᛁᚾᚢᚾᚴᛅᚴᛅᛒ (k-i-n-u-n-k-a-k-a-p, the k-rune writing g, the b-rune writing final p, and the doubled n written once, as runic orthography economizes geminates). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: ginnungagap.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: A void can leave no votives: Ginnungagap's evidence is entirely manuscript evidence, and unusually good of its kind. Völuspá, Vafþrúðnismál, and Grímnismál survive in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), the great Reykjavík codex that preserves nearly the whole mythological corpus; Snorri's Gylfaginning, with its systematic account of the gap, is transmitted in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (GKS 2367 4to, early 14th c.), the Codex Wormianus, and the Codex Upsaliensis, the last sometimes held to preserve an earlier redaction. No runic inscription names the compound — a silence it shares with every other item of cosmological furniture — and no picture stone can be securely read as the meeting of rime and fire, though scholars have occasionally proposed cosmic scenes among the Gotlandic imagery. The archaeology of Ginnungagap is thus the archaeology of the bookhand: a phrase in a thirteenth-century Icelandic codex, preserving the first sentence of the northern world.
